lede: A model train runs out along its track, waits, then reverses past the station. It has covered plenty of track but ended up near where it began. Average speed divides the track covered by the time; average velocity divides where it ended up, sign and all.
can: Find the total distance and the displacement of a journey, from words or from a graph.
Divide by the whole time, stops included, for an average speed or an average velocity.
Explain why the mean of two stage speeds is not the average speed.

caption: The train goes 160 m out, waits, then comes 256 m back, past the station.

md: Distance counts every metre the train covers, so it only ever grows. Displacement is where the train is now, measured from the station along the track, and it carries a sign: out is positive, so finishing past the station on the other side is negative. One journey, two different totals.

stem: The train goes 160 m out, waits, then comes 256 m back along the same track. Find its total distance and its displacement at the end.

steps.decision: Both legs count as lengths, whichever way the train was going. Nothing is taken away from a distance.
Coming back is the negative direction, so that leg is taken away. The minus says the train ends 96 m past the station, on the far side.

prompt: A trolley rolls 70 m forward along a straight corridor, then 125 m back. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
explain: A distance adds every leg as a length, whichever way the trolley rolls, so nothing is taken away: $70 + 125 = 195$ m. This is step 1 of See it. Taking the legs away gives the displacement, $-55$ m, which answers a different question.

twin.prompt: A cart is pushed 45 m along a straight path, then 95 m back. What total distance does it travel, in metres?
twin.explain: Both legs count as lengths: $45 + 95 = 140$ m. Only the displacement takes the way back away.

alt: A bar for the train's clock split into three stages: 20 seconds out, 12 seconds waiting, shaded, and 32 seconds back, 64 seconds from start to finish.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 128' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='16' y='40' width='115' height='34' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='73.5' y='62.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>20 s</text><text x='73.5' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>out</text><rect x='131' y='40' width='69' height='34' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.28' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='165.5' y='62.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>12 s</text><text x='165.5' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>wait</text><rect x='200' y='40' width='184' height='34' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='292' y='62.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>32 s</text><text x='292' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>back</text><path d='M16 90v10M384 90v10M16 95H384' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='200' y='118' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>start to finish: 64 s</text></svg>
caption: The 12 seconds of waiting are part of the train's journey.

md: Average speed $= \dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$. The time underneath is the whole journey, from the first second to the last, and a stop counts: the train really did take 64 seconds to cover its 416 m.

title: What an average speed says
md: It is the one steady speed that would cover the same distance in the same time. The train moves at 8 m/s whenever it moves, yet its average speed is lower, because for 12 seconds it covers nothing.

stem: Find the train's average speed: 160 m out in 20 s, a 12 s wait, then 256 m back in 32 s.

steps.decision: Both legs as lengths. On the paper this line carries the first mark.
Every stage of the clock goes in, the wait included.
One division, total over total. The second mark is for this line.

prompt: A bus drives 1400 m in 100 s, waits 30 s at a stop, then drives 1300 m in 140 s, all in the same direction along a straight road. What is its average speed, in m/s?
explain: An average speed is one division, total distance over total time, and the wait belongs in the time: $2700 \div 270 = 10$ m/s. This is step 3 of See it. Leaving out the 30 s gives about $11.25$ m/s, which is too big.

twin.prompt: A cyclist rides 700 m in 60 s, stops for 30 s, then rides 740 m in 70 s in the same direction. What is her average speed, in m/s?
twin.explain: Total distance 1440 m over the whole 160 s, the stop included: $1440 \div 160 = 9$ m/s.

text: Why not average the two speeds

alt: Two bars side by side for one journey: 15 seconds at 14 metres per second, then 35 seconds, shaded, at 6 metres per second. The same 210 metres each.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 128' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='16' y='40' width='110.4' height='34' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.08' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='71.2' y='62.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>15 s</text><text x='71.2' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>14 m/s</text><rect x='126.4' y='40' width='257.6' height='34' fill='currentColor' fill-opacity='0.28' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='255.2' y='62.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>35 s</text><text x='255.2' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>6 m/s</text><path d='M16 90v10M384 90v10M16 95H384' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='200' y='118' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>the same 210 m each, not the same time</text></svg>
caption: Equal distances, unequal times: the slow stage lasts longer, so it counts for more.

md: Two stages at 14 m/s and 6 m/s average 10 m/s only if they last equally long. Equal distances do not take equal times: the slow stage lasts longer, so it pulls the average speed towards its own speed. Work from the totals and the weighting takes care of itself.

stem: A cyclist rides 210 m at 14 m/s, then 210 m at 6 m/s along a straight path. Find her average speed.

steps.decision: Each stage's time is its distance divided by its speed.
Add the distances and add the times.
Not 10: the slow stage lasted more than twice as long, so it counts for more.

prompt: A runner covers 500 m at 10 m/s, then 500 m at 2.5 m/s. What is her average speed?
explain: Equal distances, unequal times: $500 \div 10 = 50$ s and $500 \div 2.5 = 200$ s, so $1000 \div 250 = 4$ m/s. This is See it again, steps 1 to 3. 6.25 is the mean of the speeds, and 12.5 their sum.

twin.prompt: A rower covers 350 m at 7 m/s, then 350 m at 2.5 m/s. What is her average speed?
twin.explain: Times $50$ s and $140$ s, so $700 \div 190 = 3.68$ m/s. 4.75 is the mean of the two speeds, which ignores the times.

optionNotes.why: The mean of 7 and 2.5 ignores that the slow half takes 140 s against 50 s.
A sum of two speeds is not a speed of the journey; divide the total distance by the total time.
It is the mean of 10 and 2.5, which feels fair, but she spends 200 s on the slow half and only 50 s on the fast one, so the slow speed counts for more.
Adding the two speeds seems to combine the stages, but a sum of speeds is not the speed of any journey: total distance over total time is.

alt: A straight canal seen from above with a lock marked at 0. The float starts at plus 40 metres, east of the lock, and one arrow shows it drifting west to minus 25 metres.
svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 154' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><path d='M18 96H382' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M26 22h34' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M64 22l-9 -4.5v9Z' fill='currentColor'/><text x='72' y='27' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>east is positive</text><path d='M319.1 76H89.9' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2.2'/><path d='M80.9 76l11 -5.5v11Z' fill='currentColor'/><circle cx='319.1' cy='76' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='200' y='68' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>the drift</text><path d='M319.1 76V96M80.9 76V96' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3' stroke-opacity='0.55'/><path d='M172.5 89v14' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='172.5' y='122' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>lock</text><path d='M319.1 89v14' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='319.1' y='122' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>+40</text><path d='M80.9 89v14' fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='80.9' y='122' text-anchor='middle' font-size='15' fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit'>−25</text></svg>
caption: East of the lock is positive, so a finish to the west is negative.

md: Average velocity $= \dfrac{\text{total displacement}}{\text{total time}}$: the same clock underneath, a different quantity on top. Displacement is finish minus start, so it is zero when a body comes back to its start and negative when it finishes on the far side. The train's is $-96 \div 64 = -1.5$ m/s.

stem: A float drifts along a straight canal. It starts 40 m east of a lock, and 50 s later it is 25 m west of the lock. Taking east as positive, find its average velocity.

steps.decision: West of the lock is the negative side, so the finish carries a minus.
Finish minus start: the float has moved 65 m west.
Displacement over time. The minus sign is part of the answer: the float drifted west.

prompt: A buoy is 18 m north of a jetty. 25 s later it has drifted to 22 m south of the jetty. Taking north as positive, what is its average velocity?
explain: Displacement is finish minus start, with south negative: $-22 - 18 = -40$ m, and $-40 \div 25 = -1.6$ m/s. This is steps 2 and 3 of See it. Without the minus the direction is lost; using the finish alone forgets where it started.

twin.prompt: A kayak is 30 m east of a buoy. 20 s later it is 14 m west of the buoy. Taking east as positive, what is its average velocity?
twin.explain: Finish minus start: $-14 - 30 = -44$ m, over 20 s gives $-2.2$ m/s. The minus says it moved west.

optionNotes.why: The size is right, but the kayak ends west of the buoy, the negative side, so the minus stays.
That divides the finish alone; the kayak started 30 m east, and displacement is finish minus start.
Adding the start to the finish runs the subtraction the wrong way; take the start away from the finish.
The size is right, but the buoy ends on the south side, the negative one, so its velocity keeps the minus.
Dividing the finish, −22 m, by the time forgets that the buoy started 18 m north; displacement is finish minus start.
Adding −22 and 18 treats the start the wrong way round; displacement takes the start away: −22 − 18 = −40.

md: When the answer line says m/s, every length goes into metres and every time into seconds before anything is divided. Kilometres over seconds gives a number a thousand times too small. A speed in km/h is kilometres per hour: 54 km/h is 54000 m in 3600 s, which is 15 m/s.

title: Kilometres are GCSE Mathematics
md: No FM2 paper from 2019 to 2026 gives a length in km or a time in minutes: this is a GCSE Mathematics skill, kept here because it trips answers. Metres and seconds are the units of this unit.

stem: A cyclist covers 2.7 km along a straight road in 7.5 minutes. Find her average speed in m/s.

steps.decision: A kilometre is 1000 m. Change the length first.
A minute is 60 s. Now both are in the answer line's units.
Divide only once both are converted.

title: Speed, Distance and Time
why: The GCSE arithmetic underneath, done slowly: watch the units fixed before the division rather than after it.

prompt: A skier covers 1.62 km in 3 minutes. What is her average speed, in m/s?
explain: Metres over seconds: $1.62$ km is $1620$ m and 3 minutes is $180$ s, so $1620 \div 180 = 9$ m/s. This is See it, steps 1 to 3. Dividing $1.62$ by 180 mixes kilometres with seconds and gives a number a thousand times too small.

twin.prompt: A runner covers 0.96 km in 4 minutes. What is her average speed, in m/s?
twin.explain: $0.96$ km is $960$ m and 4 minutes is $240$ s, so $960 \div 240 = 4$ m/s.

text: Reading the totals off a graph

md: On a displacement/time graph the height is the displacement. Each sloping stretch is a leg: its length is how far the line rises or falls, and a level stretch is a stop. The distance adds those lengths; the displacement is the last height minus the first; the time is where the journey ends on the time axis.

stem: The displacement/time graph shows a robot's journey along a straight corridor. Find its average speed and its average velocity.

figure.alt: A displacement/time graph: a straight line from (0, 0) up to (20, 100), level to (30, 100), then down to (50, −30), crossing the time axis.

steps.working: Legs: up $100$ m, level, down $130$ m (from $100$ to $-30$)
steps.decision: Read each sloping stretch as a length. The falling leg crosses zero, so it is 100 down to zero and 30 more.
Both lengths added, whichever way the line slopes.
The journey ends at 50 s on the time axis; the 10 s level stretch is inside that.
Last height minus first height, over the same time. It ends below zero, so it is negative.

prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 40 m over the first 10 s, stays level for 10 s, then falls to −20 m at 50 s. What is the average speed, in m/s?
explain: Read the legs as lengths: up 40, then down from 40 to $-20$, which is 60. Distance $40 + 60 = 100$ m over the whole 50 s gives 2 m/s. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it. Taking the last height, $-20$, as the distance loses the first leg.

twin.prompt: A displacement/time graph rises from 0 m to 36 m over the first 12 s, stays level for 8 s, then falls to −24 m at 50 s. What is the average speed, in m/s?
twin.explain: Up 36, then down from 36 to $-24$, which is 60: $96 \div 50 = 1.92$ m/s.

md: **Draw it, then divide** (Summer 2024). The part before asks you to draw the journey's displacement/time graph. Take the legs from your own graph; if the body ends somewhere other than its start, its displacement is not zero.
**A late start** (Summer 2023). Two journeys share one clock and one sets off later. Its time is its own finish minus its own start, never the reading where its line ends.
**Speed, in bold** (Summer 2019). When a velocity has just been found, a bold **speed** asks for its size, without the sign. Answer the word the question prints.

stem: A cart waits at O until $t = 6$ s, travels 175 m to A by $t = 31$ s, waits until $t = 38$ s, then comes 45 m back towards O, arriving at $t = 50$ s. Find its average speed.

steps.decision: The first line to write: the legs as lengths. It carries the first mark.
Its own finish minus its own start. The clock reads 50 at the end, but the cart only set off at 6 s.
Dividing by 50 would give about 4.4 m/s, the late-start slip.
It ends between O and A, not back at O, so an average velocity here would not be zero.

prompt: A two-mark part asks for the average speed of a journey you have just drawn on a displacement/time graph. What do you write first?
options: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
The displacement at the end, over the time
answer: The total distance and the total time, on two lines
explain: The marks follow the lines: the first mark is for a correct total distance, the second mark for dividing it by the whole time, so write those two totals first. This is steps 1 and 2 of See it. Stage speeds lead to the averaging trap, and the displacement belongs to a velocity.

optionNotes.why: Stage speeds feel like progress, but they lead straight to averaging them, and the marks are for the totals.

optionNotes.option: The displacement at the end, over the time
optionNotes.why: That is the first line of an average velocity; a speed question wants the distance, every leg added.
An answer first looks quick, but if it is wrong nothing written has earned a mark; the totals come first.

prompt: Two journeys share one clock. A van sets off at t = 15 s and finishes at t = 75 s, covering 480 m. What is its average speed, in m/s?
explain: Its time is its own journey: finish minus start, $75 - 15 = 60$ s, so $480 \div 60 = 8$ m/s. This is step 2 of See it. Dividing by the clock reading, 75, gives 6.4 m/s: the late start the Summer 2023 examiners saw candidates miss.

twin.prompt: Two journeys share one clock. A bike sets off at t = 20 s and stops at t = 100 s, covering 360 m. What is its average speed, in m/s?
twin.explain: Its own time is $100 - 20 = 80$ s, so $360 \div 80 = 4.5$ m/s.

md:
Add every leg as a length for the distance; take finish minus start for the displacement.
Divide by the whole time, stops included, counted from the body's own start.
Say why the mean of two stage speeds is not the average speed.
Put lengths in metres and times in seconds before dividing.
Give an average velocity with its sign: zero if the body returns to its start.

Average speed has been a two-mark part straight after drawing a displacement/time graph (Summer 2024): the first mark for the total distance, the second for dividing by the whole time, stops included. Average velocity can be asked too: put the displacement on top and keep its sign. Stuck? Write total distance over total time as a fraction first.
